The future of the British Empire must be regarded as extremely problematical. No man can foretell what will be the condition of Great Britain a hundred years hence. We can only judge of the probabilities of the case, by considering what has happened in similar instances. turns: What is the future of the British Empire?
answers: The British Empire must continue to exist so long as the mother country and the colonies are mutually advantageous to each other. The bond which at present unites them can only be broken by the consent of both parties to the compact, and until that consent has been given, speculation as to the future must be idle and unprofitable. The mother country and the colonies can scarcely fail to be mutually advantageous to each other, so long as the former remains the greatest manufacturing, and the latter the greatest agricultural, state in the world. The profits arising from the exchange of their surplus productions must be reciprocal. The mother country must continue to derive food from the colonies, and the colonies must continue to receive manufactures from the mother country. The bond of union can only be severed by the direct interposition of divine Providence. Should the time ever arrive when the prosperity of Great Britain shall decline, and her manufactures cease to afford a profitable field of employment to her people, the bond must be broken, and the colonies will become independent states. On the other hand, should the colonies cease to prosper, and to afford a field of emigration to the surplus population of the mother country, the bond must be broken, and Great Britain must lose her dependencies. At present, however, there exists no symptom of the decline of British prosperity, and, consequently, no indication of the severance of the colonial tie. The imperial connection may, therefore, be regarded as permanent.
